title: Amos 2:1–5
context: The LORD speaks against Moab for burning the bones of Edom’s king into lime, a wrong done not to Israel but to another nation, and against Judah for rejecting the LORD’s law and following lies. The charge against Judah differs from those against the nations because it concerns God’s revealed law. The incident behind the Moab oracle and the location of Kerioth are uncertain. Shared ground: both traditions see God’s justice extending to all peoples, and those who have received his law are held to account for it.

verses.text: The LORD says: “For three transgressions of Moab, yes, for four, I will not turn away its punishment, because he burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime;
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says Moab will be punished because he burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime. Arminian readers see desecration of the dead condemned.

Notably, the wrong is done to Edom, not Israel.
verses.reformedNotes:
Scripture does not narrate this incident elsewhere, and its occasion is uncertain.

Reformed readers see God’s justice extending to wrongs between nations. Shared ground: God cares about dignity even toward an enemy’s remains.

verses.text: but I will send a fire on Moab, and it will devour the palaces of Kerioth; and Moab will die with tumult, with shouting, and with the sound of the trumpet;
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will send fire on Moab and devour the palaces of Kerioth; Moab will die amid tumult, shouting, and trumpet. Arminian readers see judgment answering Moab’s contempt for the dead.

The scene is one of battle.
verses.reformedNotes:
Kerioth is generally taken as a Moabite town, though its location is uncertain.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereign judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read this as judgment on Moab, with the site held cautiously.

verses.text: and I will cut off the judge from among them, and will kill all its princes with him,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will cut off Moab’s judge and kill its princes with him. The leadership falls.

Arminian readers see accountability extending to those who governed the nation and shaped its actions.
verses.reformedNotes:
The word “judge” may refer to Moab’s chief ruler; the text does not explain the title.

Reformed readers see God’s rule over all leaders. Shared ground: both traditions read this as God’s judgment on Moab’s rulers, completing the oracles against the surrounding nations.

verses.text: The LORD says: “For three transgressions of Judah, yes, for four, I will not turn away its punishment, because they have rejected the LORD’s law, and have not kept his statutes, and their lies have led them astray, after which their fathers walked;
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says Judah will be punished “because they have rejected the LORD’s law, and have not kept his statutes.” Arminian readers see a covenant people held to a higher standard.

Their lies, followed by their fathers, have led them astray.
verses.reformedNotes:
Judah’s charge differs from the nations’: it concerns God’s revealed law.

Reformed readers see covenant privilege bringing greater accountability. Shared ground: those who receive God’s law answer for rejecting it.

verses.text: but I will send a fire on Judah, and it will devour the palaces of Jerusalem.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will send fire on Judah and devour the palaces of Jerusalem. Judah receives the same refrain as the nations.

Arminian readers see that covenant status does not exempt Judah from the consequences of rejecting God’s law.
verses.reformedNotes:
The repetition places Judah alongside the surrounding nations in judgment.

Reformed readers see God’s impartial justice. Shared ground: both traditions read this as a warning that God’s people are not shielded from judgment, which prepares for the oracle against Israel.
